# Quantization

Also called: Quantization with Matrix

## Overview
Quantization is a lossy compression technique that maps continuous or high-precision volume data to a discrete, lower-precision domain to reduce storage and transmission costs [S1][S3, unofficial][S5]. It solves the problem of storing large volumetric datasets by exploiting redundancy in values, either through spatial grouping (Vector Quantization), local scaling (Scalar Quantization), or structural mapping (Neural Implicit Compression) [S1][S3, unofficial][S5]. Unlike [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md), which processes values independently within blocks, [Vector Quantization](907-vector-quantization.md) groups data to capture correlations, while [Differentiable Quantization for Neural Fields](10195-differentiable-quantization-for-neural-fields.md) integrates discretization into the training loop to preserve model quality [S1][S3, unofficial][S5].

Not given in the sources.

## Subtopics

### [Vector Quantization](907-vector-quantization.md)
Vector Quantization (VQ) maps $n$-dimensional input vectors to a single fixed-length index referencing an entry in a pre-defined or learned codebook. It solves the problem of storing large volumetric datasets by exploiting spatial redundancy: identical or similar data blocks are replaced by compact indices, allowing for extremely fast decompression on the GPU. Unlike [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md), which processes values independently, VQ groups data into blocks to capture correlations, and unlike [Hierarchical Vector Quantization](827-hierarchical-vector-quantization.md), it typically employs a single resolution level codebook.

### [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md)
Scalar quantization (per-block) is a lossy compression technique that maps high-precision volume data to a lower-precision discrete domain by computing local minimum and maximum values for each data block, alongside a local index for every element within that block. It solves the problem of random-access decompression in GPU-based direct volume rendering by enabling parallel reconstruction of voxel values on-the-fly without decompressing the entire volume into main memory. Unlike general-purpose codecs, it is a simple, hardware-friendly method where the reconstruction error is directly controlled by the number of bits allocated to the local index.

### [Chroma Subsampling](6512-chroma-subsampling.md)
Chroma subsampling for volumetric data reduces the bitrate of color information by lowering the resolution of chrominance components (U, V) while maintaining luminance (Y) at full resolution. Unlike direct subsampling, which causes significant information loss in sparse volumetric representations, this method defines one color value for every eight adjacent corners of a voxel grid, preserving color quality at low bitrates. It is distinct from sibling methods like Scalar Quantization because it operates on the spatial arrangement of existing voxels to determine color validity, rather than merely reducing precision of existing values.

### [Differentiable Quantization for Neural Fields](10195-differentiable-quantization-for-neural-fields.md)
Differentiable quantization reduces the memory footprint of neural field representations (such as 3D Gaussian Splatting or NeRF grids) by mapping continuous parameters to single-byte integers during the training process. Unlike post-training quantization, which causes quality degradation due to the mismatch between the optimized continuous model and the discrete inference model, this method integrates quantization into the optimization loop. It sets itself apart from standard scalar quantization by using a straight-through estimator to allow gradients to flow through the non-differentiable rounding operation, ensuring the network learns values that are robust to discretization.

### [Neural Implicit Network Compression](10414-neural-implicit-network-compression.md)
Neural Implicit Network Compression (often referred to as neurcomp) is a method for compressing scientific volume data by training a coordinate-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to map spatial coordinates directly to field values. It serves as both compressed storage and a queryable data source, eliminating the need for full decoding before visualization. Unlike traditional lossy compressors (e.g., SZ, ZFP) that produce bitstreams requiring full decoding, or tensor decomposition methods (e.g., TTHRESH) that struggle at high compression ratios, neurcomp uses a SIREN architecture with residual connections and weight quantization to achieve superior reconstruction quality at extreme compression ratios. It sets itself apart from siblings like [Differentiable Quantization for Neural Fields](10195-differentiable-quantization-for-neural-fields.md) by focusing on scientific volume fidelity and specific weight quantization techniques (k-means) rather than general differentiable quantization schemes for neural fields.

### [Unquantization Functions](13872-unquantization-functions.md)
Unquantization functions convert integer quantized values back to half-precision float range, serving as the inverse operation to the quantization step in transform-based volume data compression. Unlike general scalar quantization which maps continuous domains to discrete indices, these specific functions are tailored for the BC6H compression format used in real-time graphics, handling specific bit-depths (7, 9, 10) to reconstruct floating-point color or density values from compressed integer representations.

### [Global Quantization](15134-global-quantization.md)
Global quantization is a compression strategy for neural volume representations that maintains a single shared parameter table for all independent small Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) within a specific scale, rather than quantizing each network locally. It solves the redundancy problem where distinct spatial blocks often contain similar content, allowing multiple MLPs to map to the same set of floating-point parameters. This approach achieves higher compression ratios than local quantization while maintaining comparable reconstruction accuracy.

### Lossy Quantization for Coarsened Patches
Lossy compression for coarsened patches in the bintree hierarchy. Quantization error $q$ is proportional to coarsening error $c$: $q = qc$, where $q$ is a fixed constant usually $< 1$. A single unified error is recomputed and nested for each patch. Quantization levels are restricted to power-of-two multiples of vertical resolution $\Delta z$ for efficient bit-shift implementation. Shift $k$ is calculated as: $k = \lceil \log_2(\epsilon_q / \Delta z) \rceil + 1$ if $\epsilon_q \ge \Delta z$, else $0$. All finest level vertices have zero shift. Vertices classified as boundary (corners $C$, legs $L$, hypotenuse $H$) and interior $I$. Corners stored at full precision. Quantization of original height values (not residuals) ensures adjacent patches agree on shared boundaries [S2].

### HSV Colour Sorting
A technique to preserve colour quality during DXT1 compression by reordering colours based on HSV values [S3, unofficial]. The effectiveness of HSV sorting depends on which component (H, S, or V) is the most frequent in the voxel data’s set of colours [S3, unofficial].

### Interpolation Symmetry Quantization
A method to improve the accuracy of quantized weights by exploiting the symmetry of linear interpolation between segments [S4]. Quantize both $w$ and $1 - w$ using the codebook generated by the scalar quantizer. Keep the representation resulting in the lower error. Store either $(i, j, w)$ or $(j, i, 1 - w)$ in the output stream. Linear interpolation: $(1 - w)s_i + w s_j$, where $(i, j, w)$ is equivalent to $(j, i, 1 - w)$ [S4].

### Position Lattice Quantization
An attempted method to compress Gaussian positions by quantizing them to a lattice structure and embedding positional constraints into the training process [S5]. Fails to compress positions without introducing significant rendering error [S5]. Identified as a future research direction for end-to-end positional compression [S5].

### Post-finetune Refinement
A refinement step that uses a small number of bits to enhance the reconstruction quality of important voxels, compensating for losses introduced by coarse quantization [S6]. Ablation study on Synthetic-NeRF dataset shows disabling post-finetune causes a -1.72 dB $\Delta$PSNR, -0.07 $\Delta$SSIM, and -0.079 MB $\Delta$Size [S6]. Disabling post-finetune saves bits but inevitably deteriorates rendering quality, confirming its necessity for maintaining RD performance [S6].

## Background
Quantization in volume rendering has evolved from simple scalar methods to complex, differentiable techniques integrated into neural representations. Early methods focused on scalar quantization for direct volume rendering to enable random access [S2][S3, unofficial]. With the rise of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting, quantization has shifted towards weight and grid value compression, requiring differentiable estimators to maintain training stability [S1, S5]. Specific applications include streaming free-viewpoint videos using 3D DCT coefficient quantization [S1], terrain compression using coarsened patches [S2], and voxel animation sequences using HSV sorting [S3, unofficial].
